title: Beat the trivial x^{1/4} gap between sums of two squares
credit: Classical; stated as open in A. Kalmynin, 'Intervals between numbers that are sums of two squares' (arXiv:1706.07380).
premise_risks: Kalmynin's statement is from 2017–18; I found no later improvement but a 2025–26 claim in a non-indexed venue cannot be excluded
plain: Let R(x) be the largest gap between consecutive integers of the form a²+b² up to x. A greedy argument (take the largest square below n, then fix the remainder with a second square) gives R(x) <= C·x^{1/4}, and this exponent has never been improved, although gaps are believed to be only about log x in size. Prove that R(x) is eventually smaller than any constant multiple of x^{1/4}.
math: Let $S=\{a^2+b^2: a,b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\}$. Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $X_0$ such that for all real $x\ge X_0$ the interval $(x,\,x+\varepsilon x^{1/4}]$ meets $S$; equivalently, the maximal gap between consecutive elements of $S\cap[1,x]$ is $o(x^{1/4})$.
